title: ‘By Any Means’ Review: Mark Wahlberg Teaches the Virtues of Violence in Elegance Bratton’s Bluntly Drawn Historical Thriller
description: In Peter Farrelly’s “Green Book,” Viggo Mortensen’s driver famously introduces Mahersahala Ali’s concert pianist to fried chicken. The white man, an
body:
In Peter Farrelly’s “Green Book,” Viggo Mortensen’s driver famously introduces Mahersahala Ali’s concert pianist to fried chicken. The white man, an expert, proves his cultural bona fides to the Black protagonist, the student. The pair of outsiders share a moment of bonding, and America’s wounds are salved. 

	That movie felt dated in 2018. Eight years later, “By Any Means,” the second feature directed by Elegance Bratton, plays like a downright relic. Equally egregious in its vision of racial healing and even less watchable on a scene-to-scene basis, this new film similarly involves a white man edifying his starchier Black associate, although here, the lesson is not in the culinary arts, but in the art of ruthless violence.
	

	Set in 1960s Mississippi, the film opens with an archival montage establishing the disappearance of three civil rights workers during Freedom Summer. Two of the men were Jewish, one was Black, and all three were working to register local Black voters. The historical media clips conclude with the search still underway and authorities vowing to find the men and bring those responsible to justice.


	Cut to Mark Wahlberg, muscles bulging and hair absurdly parted, in a dingy basement, beating a man to the brink of death. “Where are the bodies?” he demands, swinging a baseball bat into his bloody victim’s already pulverized knees. 

	So begins a streak of brutal and relentless violence taken brutally and relentlessly seriously. Based on a true story, the film tracks Wahlberg’s character, the mob enforcer Greg Scarpa, as he teams up with FBI Agent Wayne Strider, played by Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. The pair are tasked with investigating the murder of local NAACP chapter president Vernon Dahmer (Giancarlo Esposito) by members of the Ku Klux Klan — though they have starkly different ideas about how to get the job done.
	

	Here’s where the title comes in. Wayne, who confronts the cruel effects of white supremacy daily on the job, believes in working within the system. He became an agent to uphold the law, and prefers to play things by the book. Greg has no such allegiance. Quietly enlisted by Wayne’s superiors, the mob muscle operates by a simpler principle: Information should be obtained by any means necessary, including, and especially, clobbering it out of potential sources.

	That phrase — “by any means necessary” — was, of course, popularized and embodied by the Black activist Malcolm X, and its implicit transfer here to Greg is just one instance of the film’s crude rewriting of history. It opens by claiming that its events are based on a true story, but that isn’t exactly the case: While Greg Scarpa was a real mobster likely deployed by the FBI on the sly, there is no evidence that he worked with a Black handler, and Wayne Strider is an invented character.

	Regardless: this is a movie, and its particular brand of movie magic lies in repurposing familiar tropes into a gripping action thriller. As the men go about their investigation, driving around the city and interrogating locals, those tropes come to include white saviordom, but also the more pedestrian mismatched buddy duo, in which comedy and drama derive from the men’s clashing sensibilities beyond their approach to violence.

	Wayne, who trained in Chicago before moving home to Mississippi, is a buttoned-up instrument of the federal government, and though he has a rough edge — at one point, he punches a filing cabinet in frustration — he is nearly prim in his fidelity to the letter of the law. He’s also devoted to his wife (Nicole Beharie, doing a lot with a little), who spends much of her screen time quietly affirming him, rubbing his neck or exchanging a heartfelt look.

	Greg, from Brooklyn, offers some comedy by contrast. To him, violence isn’t only an inevitability, but a virtue. Chewing toothpicks in a white tank top, he has a tendency to brutalize anyone who annoys him, be it a gun dealer or a highway patrol officer. And despite having a wife and kids at home — we meet them eating penne — Greg is not the family type. When Wayne drives to retrieve him from a motel, he finds Greg in bed with a giggling, blonde floozy. (As a general rule, the film’s women are broadly drawn.)
	

	The big idea of “By Any Means” is to pit Wayne’s worldview against Greg’s — essentially staging an obscenely reductive version of the debate between meeting force with nonviolent resistance and answering it in kind. But the film also wants to trace how Greg’s down-to-earth temerity rubs off on Wayne, coaxing out some of his righteous rage. “You’ve got your gun, you’ve got your badge, now you need to grow some balls,” Greg tells him in a line that the audience is meant to cheer on. Another of Greg’s moderately offensive eye-rollers: “I ain’t shining no shoes, I’m cracking heads.”

	If there’s a saving grace here, it’s Bratton’s gorgeous filmmaking, which transforms even the most sickening or obvious scenes into displays of beauty. Working with the cinematographer Ante Cheng, Bratton makes lovely use of light. In one wide shot, dawn sunlight glances off wet pavement; in another, introducing the villains, hostile faces are cast in sinister horizontal shadows from window shutters.

	The images have a subtlety sorely lacking in the film surrounding them, and leave us longing for a story more worthy of Bratton’s eye. His debut feature, “The Inspection,” was a lovely, lyrical portrait of a Marine in training; its ingenuity suggests that the problems of “By Any Means” — written by Sascha Penn from a script that previously appeared on the Black List — were baked in prior to Bratton’s involvement. The most fundamental of those problems is apparent from the opening scene: For a movie that purports to weigh opposing attitudes toward violence, “By Any Means” has already chosen a side.

schema.headline: ‘By Any Means’ Review: Mark Wahlberg Teaches the Virtues of Violence in Elegance Bratton’s Bluntly Drawn Historical Thriller

title: ‘Lanterns’ Episode 3 Attracts 10 Million Viewers Globally on HBO Max, a New Series High
description: HBO Max‘s “Lanterns” continues to grow in viewership. The DC Studios series’ third episode, which premiered Sunday, Aug. 30, averaged 10 million vie
body:
HBO Max‘s “Lanterns” continues to grow in viewership. The DC Studios series’ third episode, which premiered Sunday, Aug. 30, averaged 10 million viewers globally and 7 million viewers in the U.S. after three days of viewership, according to the network/streamer. 

	That marks a series high for “Lanterns,” which continues to grow week-to-week since its series premiere on August 16. Also, per HBO Max, the show’s pilot episode has now attracted more than 20 million viewers worldwide.
	

	HBO Max also reports that “Lanterns” is now among the top five series launches in the platform’s history. It also remains the biggest premiere for a DC Studios show on HBO Max. 


	Episode 3 of “Lanterns” dove into the backstory of John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) and how long he has been preparing and training — at the direction of his parents — to one day take over the role of the Green Lantern from Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler). In the episode, John is grilled by one of the Guardians (Laura Linney) to see whether he’s worthy of replacing Hal.

	Through flashbacks, we see how his father, John Stewart, Sr. (J. Alphonse Nicholson), and mother Bernadette (Jasmine Cephas Jones) train him to show no fear.

	Based on DC’s “Green Lantern” comic books, “Lanterns” stars Pierre, Chandler, Kelly Macdonald, Garret Dillahunt, Poorna Jagannathan, Jason Ritter and Ulrich Thomsen. 

	Per the official logline, the show follows “new recruit John Stewart (Pierre) and Lantern legend Hal Jordan (Chandler), two intergalactic cops drawn into a dark, earth-based mystery as they investigate a murder in the American heartland.”
	

	“Lanterns” is co-written by Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof, and Tom King. All three serve as executive producers along with James Hawes, with Hawes also directing the first two episodes. James Gunn, Peter Safran and Ron Schmidt also executive produce. Stephen Williams, Geeta Vasant Patel and Alik Sakharov will direct on the series. HBO produces in association with Warner Bros. Television and DC Studios.

schema.headline: ‘Lanterns’ Episode 3 Attracts 10 Million Viewers Globally on HBO Max, a New Series High

title: ‘Dungeons & Dragons’ Live-Action Series ‘Ravenloft’ Set at Netflix After ‘Forgotten Realms’ Project Scrapped
description: A new live-action “Dungeons & Dragons” TV series is in the works at Netflix based on the iconic franchise’s popular gothic-horror setting “Ravenloft
body:
A new live-action “Dungeons & Dragons” TV series is in the works at Netflix based on the iconic franchise’s popular gothic-horror setting “Ravenloft.”

	As this series goes into development in collaboration with the Hasbro-owned “D&D” maker Wizards of the Coast, Netflix has scrapped another “D&D” project inspired by the tabletop roleplaying game’s “The Forgotten Realms” storyline, which spans thousands of years of in-universe plot told across hundreds of gameplay books.
	

	From creator John August and executive producer Alfonso Cuarón, the “Ravenloft” series is described as a “prestige fantasy series where adventure collides with gothic horror and tragic romance, Ravenloft and its Domains of Dread redefine adventure through character-driven stories of dark magic and supernatural intrigue. At the heart of the series, Ravenloft follows the making of the vampire Darklord Strahd von Zarovich, whose story of power, love, obsession, and undead transformation charts his origins from tragic antihero to one of Dungeons & Dragons’ most notorious villains.”


	Along with August and Cuarón, “Ravenloft” is executive produced by Gabriel Marano for Hasbro, Richard Schwartz, and Gaby Rodriguez for Esperanto Filmoj.

	Launched in 1983 by creators Tracy and Laura Hickman, “Ravenloft” is one of the most played settings in the “D&D” universe and has inspired novels, tabletop RPG modules, video games and companion rulebooks.

	Recently, Wizards of the Coast released “Ravenloft: The Horrors Within,” an expanded and updated reimagining of the original storyline. The “Ravenloft” setting was featured on the first season of the Wizards-produced “D&D” actual-play TV show, “Dungeon Masters,” which debuted in April.

schema.headline: ‘Dungeons & Dragons’ Live-Action Series ‘Ravenloft’ Set at Netflix After ‘Forgotten Realms’ Project Scrapped

title: ‘Furious’ Hits 43 Million Hours Viewed in Total, With Finale Jumping 90% From Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
The Hulu crime drama “Furious” has cleared 43 million hours watched since it premiered, according to Disney.

	Starring Emmy Rossum as an FBI agent
body:
The Hulu crime drama “Furious” has cleared 43 million hours watched since it premiered, according to Disney.

	Starring Emmy Rossum as an FBI agent investigating a female serial killer (Lola Petticrew), the Elizabeth Meriwether-created series achieved that in about five weeks, having debuted on July 27. The 43 million hour-total translates to roughly 6.2 million estimated “views,” a statistic calculated by dividing total time watched by runtime. Because the first three episodes have had since late July to accrue viewership whereas the finale has been available for less than a week, the number of discrete viewers who have tuned into “Furious” at any point is likely much higher than 6.2 million, and the view count will continue to rise as people catch up to the finale.
	

	Disney also reports that the finale saw a staggering 90% more views after one day of availability than the premiere did, indicating that “Furious” was a strong word-of-mouth hit that saw significant growth over the course of Season 1, rather than stagnating or dropping off after its debut.


	The news follows the debut of “Furious” on Nielsen’s weekly streaming rankings, which operate on a four-week delay. The series opened as the No. 10 most-watched streaming original of the week of July 27-Aug. 2, at which point only three episodes were available, and will inevitably climb higher as Nielsen’s measurement catches up to the rest of Season 1.

	“Furious” has already been renewed for a second season. The series has achieved critical acclaim in addition to strong viewership, hitting a 98% on Rotten Tomatoes. “The age of QAnon may be addicted to stories about trafficking and children in danger, but ‘Furious’ is at its best when pushing past the buzzwords for an unflinching look at those affected, warts and all,” wrote Variety critic Alison Herman.
	

	In an interview with Variety, Meriwether said that Season 2 would likely follow Alice (Rossum) and her boss, Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine), working on a new case in the C20 unit, which investigates sex crimes.

schema.headline: ‘Furious’ Hits 43 Million Hours Viewed in Total, With Finale Jumping 90% From Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Season 2 Casts Milla Jovovich, Kevin Zegers and Paul Gross
description:
The cast of “Heated Rivalry” continues to warm up.

	Kevin Zegers, Paul Gross and Milla Jovovich have joined the hit ice-hockey romance series from
body:
The cast of “Heated Rivalry” continues to warm up.

	Kevin Zegers, Paul Gross and Milla Jovovich have joined the hit ice-hockey romance series from Crave ahead of its Season 2 debut on HBO Max in spring 2027.

	Zegers (“The Madison,” “Transamerica”) will play Coach Wiebe. Gross (“Good Night, and Good Luck,” “Tales of the City”) is Commissioner Roger Crowell. And Jovovich (“Resident Evil, The Fifth Element”) will portray Dr. Galina Molchalina.
	

	They join series leads Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams, as well as previously announced cast Justice Smith, Charlie Gillespie, Daniel Diemer, Shaheen Jafargholi, Robert Naylor, Sophie Nélisse, Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova, Edvin Ryding, François Arnaud, Christina Chang, Dylan Walsh, Robbie G.K., Callan Potter, Benjamin Roy, Kamilla Kowal, Emily Hampshire, Sabrina Jalees and Priyanka. 


	Created by Jacob Tierney, “Heated Rivalry” follows the skate-crossed love affair between rival hockey players Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Storrie). The two star athletes are pulled together by ambition and attraction, and what begins as a secret fling between two fresh-faced rookies develops into a years-long journey of love, denial and self-discovery.

	The show is based on Rachel Reid’s “Game Changers” book series, with the second season borrowing its premise from the sixth book, titled “The Long Game.” It follows Shane and Ilya as they play on teams that are closer geographically and navigate the complexities of taking their relationship public.

	While “Heated Rivalry” hails from the Canadian streaming service Crave, it became a massive hit months after its U.S. debut on HBO Max. The show hit the American streamer in November 2025 but became a word-of-mouth hit in early 2026, with episodes reaching an average viewership of more than 10 million.
	

	“Heated Rivalry” is commissioned by Bell Media’s Crave with the participation of the Canada Media Fund (CMF). Tierney is the writer, director and executive producer. Brendan Brady and Jayme Alter Wilson serve as executive producers. Lori Fischburg and Liane Cunje are producers, with Rachel Reid as consulting producer. Mike Goldbach serves as co-writer on Season 2.

schema.headline: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Season 2 Casts Milla Jovovich, Kevin Zegers and Paul Gross

title: ‘Too Much Sugar’ Review: Robert Greene’s Playful, High-Energy Doc Marshals a Revealing Family Moviemaking Project
description: Everyone’s a main character in “Too Much Sugar,” a scrappy, agitated, spikily entertaining study of an extended family with a whole community’s wort
body:
Everyone’s a main character in “Too Much Sugar,” a scrappy, agitated, spikily entertaining study of an extended family with a whole community’s worth of backstory, present-tense drama and diverging plans for the future. Only one person in it, however, has main character syndrome. That would be Ryan “Holli-wood” Hollinger, a self-styled patriarch with six children by five women, whose seemingly self-chosen nickname says much about how he perceives his place in the world — relative, at least, to the modest hand that life has dealt him as a former amateur MMA fighter and sometime carpenter in small-town Missouri. To a point, Robert Greene‘s quicksilver new documentary indulges that perception, making Ryan the star performer of a roving cinematic tour through his life and loves — until others in his shadow seize the spotlight for themselves. 
	

	And it’s there that “Too Much Sugar,” already interesting, becomes compelling, as Greene’s design for the film — a conceit that extends his ongoing fascination with performance and artifice in nonfiction cinema — slowly begins, without malice or subterfuge, to subvert Ryan’s. What begins, in his words, as an intended film “about fatherhood” turns into something less bullish and celebratory, as various people in his paternal orbit offer contrasting views on his presence, or absence, in their lives. 


	As Greene gives each participant liberty to make a short film of their choosing, and edits the results into a single spiraling, shape-shifting family portrait, “Too Much Sugar” becomes about many things besides fatherhood — among them grief, trauma, healing and liberation. With an unexpected angle of hard-won uplift, the film will likely be a crowdpleaser on the docfest circuit following its premiere in Venice’s Orizzonti sidebar: In distribution terms, it’s the kind of singular conversation piece that could attract equal interest from boutique theatrical distributors and larger streamers.
	

	Relentlessly chippy and self-aggrandizing, given to either shouting motivational slogans like “Don’t wait to be great” or wearing them brashly on T-shirts, Ryan is a tough protagonist to warm to. Greene admits as much in his voiceover at the outset, explaining how he first met Ryan at a middle-school basketball game in Moberly, Missouri, and took an immediate dislike to his loud, invasive courtside-coaching style. Two years later, Greene says, their sons were on the same basketball team, and that loathing turned to love. Minus any personal attachment, audiences may struggle to get there, but either way, he’s a forceful, charismatic figure who fills a room — a docmaker’s dream, certainly, but a challenging personality to grow up under.

	“Is my dad a narcissist?” asks one of his sons, 23-year-old Gavin, as he states his concern about Greene’s whole project — that it’s going to “validate” his father. His perception of Ryan is echoed, albeit often less directly worded, by most of his siblings, who include 25-year-old pro fighter Tray, teens Wayde and Hank, and therapy-fixated 12-year-old Bonnie. Chosen family, meanwhile, extends to Ryan’s best friend Michael, still numb with grief over the fatal shooting of his teenage son in a gang-related incident, and Michael’s smart, stoic younger daughter Auveon, who has a firm bond with the sensitive, imaginative Wayde. Holding this ragtag clan together is Amanda, Ryan’s on-off partner of 18 years, though biologically, she is mother to none of his children. A quiet, sidelined presence at first, she gradually becomes the doc’s most vital and sympathetic character — increasingly and defiantly vocal about Ryan’s history of infidelity and neglect.

	These counter-narratives emerge through the films that Greene enables his subjects to shoot themselves: resourceful shoestring productions that run the gamut from vérité self-portraiture to horror pastiche to mob thriller to elaborately plotted farce, as determined by the personalities and preoccupations of the people making them. The doc gives ample space to these movies-within-the-movie, letting them speak for themselves rather than placing them in condescending quote marks. We learn as much about each person from how they place and wield a camera as we do from the kinetically wandering cinematography by Greene’s DP Robert Kolodny, though the director’s authorial presence is deliberately diminished as “Too Much Sugar” becomes a progressively more communal effort. In addition to Ryan and his family, Greene’s students in documentary journalism at the University of Missouri contributed significantly to the production; the filmmaker’s son Wilkie composed the suitably changeable, see-sawing score.
	

	Ryan, meanwhile, learns his own lesson in collaboration and compromise, as he’s forced to acknowledge perspectives he’s previously ignored in his decidedly alpha vision of fatherly identity. As much as the film encourages its subjects to write and shoot their lives as they will, the most exhilarating developments in “Too Much Sugar” are finally unscripted ones, as the structure of Ryan’s family changes in ways he cannot anticipate or direct. Something new even from this reliably restless filmmaker, Greene’s latest is as lively and pugnacious as the man it initially scrutinizes, though with a significant jump on him in humility and human interest.

schema.headline: ‘Too Much Sugar’ Review: Robert Greene’s Playful, High-Energy Doc Marshals a Revealing Family Moviemaking Project

title: George Clooney Remembers ‘Mortgaging His House’ for ‘Good Night and Good Luck,’ Praises ‘Badass’ Wife Amal and Offers Aspiring Filmmaker a Job at Venice Masterclass
description: George Clooney, who received the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement from his “Jay Kelly” co-star Laura Dern on opening night of the 2026 Venice Fi
body:
George Clooney, who received the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement from his “Jay Kelly” co-star Laura Dern on opening night of the 2026 Venice Film Festival, sat down for a masterclass at the Lido’s Match Point Arena to look back on a career spanning nearly five decades.

	His relationship with Venice stretches back nearly three decades, beginning with “Out of Sight” and continuing with films including “Good Night, and Good Luck,” “Michael Clayton,” “Gravity,” “Suburbicon,” “Wolfs,” and, last year, Noah Baumbach’s “Jay Kelly.”
	

	During the wide-ranging talk, Clooney reminisced about the risks he took to make “Good Night, and Good Luck” two decades ago, recalling that he “mortgaged my house to make it” before bringing the film to Venice in 2005, where he watched it with an audience for the first time. 


	The story — about legendary CBS journalist Edward R. Murrow standing up to Sen. Joseph McCarthy at the height of the Red Scare — remained deeply personal to Clooney, whose father, Nick Clooney, was a journalist and news anchor. 

	He said he felt compelled to revisit the film on the stage at a moment when its themes of press freedom, political intimidation and the responsibility of journalists to challenge those in power still strike a chord.

	“When we decided to do the play and put the play back on, it felt like those words were more urgent than ever at a time when the networks were caving, and law firms were caving and universities were caving to the whims of, you know, a populist. And so I thought it was important to say those words,” he said about the Broadway adaptation. He paid tribute to his father for inspiring his activism and the launch of the Clooney Foundation, which he said has already “gotten 100 journalists out of jail.”
	

	 “When I was a kid, I was like seven or eight, believe it or not, my dad used to say to me, ‘I don’t give a shit what you do in life. I don’t care. You have one responsibility, and that is to challenge people with more power than you and to defend people with less power than you. That’s it.’”

	Clooney said the philosophy continues to shape both his activism and that of his wife, human rights lawyer Amal Clooney.

	“My wife and I spend a good portion of our lives trying to follow those same rules,” he said, pointing to people “born in a war zone,” suffering from hunger, women who are mistreated and imprisoned journalists. “Those people need some luck. And so our job is to be part of that solution.”

	Clooney also recalled his own years of campaigning to bring attention to atrocities in Darfur and admitted he hasn’t been as successful as his wife in actually bringing perpetrators to justice.

	“I had success at making it loud, but not a lot of success at making it stop, or certainly not a lot of success at bringing people to justice,” he said. “And then 20 years later, my wife finally puts some of these guys on trial and gets them thrown in jail … She got it done,” he added, calling Amal “a badass.”

	Clooney also recalled watching Amal take on the case of Nadia Murad, the Yazidi survivor of ISIS atrocities who later won the Nobel Peace Prize. When Murad first came to their home, Clooney said Amal — already overwhelmed with cases — had warned him not to let her take on another one.

	Four hours later, he found the two women sitting on the floor crying together. “I said, ‘You’re taking the case,’” Clooney recalled.

	During the panel, Clooney also passionately discussed the balance of power between an actor and his director.

	“The director is the painter and everything else is the paint,” he said. “That actor is the paint. The music is the paint. The sound design, the cinematography. Those are all paints. And the director gets to dip his brush into each one of those,” he added.

	“You know, an actor only affects it as much as the director decides,” Clooney continued. “I could change any actor’s performance as a director. I could cut them out, for that matter.”

	Clooney talked about working with Terrence Malick on “A Thin Red Line.” Malick “hadn’t worked in fifteen years and wanted to come back and do a film,” he said. “So I thought I’m going to help him get this film made, and I’m going to do this part.” Clooney traveled to Australia and shot “A Thin Red Line” for months, “and then he [Malick] cut me completely out, except the last scene in the film, the very last scene.”
	

	“And I watched it. I was like: he cut me completely out. You’ll leave me in the last scene. My God, I look like an asshole.”

	He also told the room packed with aspiring actors and filmmakers that success in Hollywood depends partly on luck — but that they can also manufacture some of their own. “You have to end up being the right person in the right place at the right time,” he said. “You can create a lot of that luck.”

	He pointed to his own career-making role as pediatrician Doug Ross on “ER,” noting that he had already appeared in seven television series before landing the NBC medical drama.

	“There is just a moment where something works. But you gotta keep chasing it,” Clooney said. “You gotta be out there and available and go, you know, ‘I’m your guy.’”

	Then, almost as if to prove his point, a 25-year-old recent film school graduate from Belgium, originally from Algeria, stood up during the Q&A and asked Clooney for a job on one of his productions. She said she hoped to become a director but wanted to gain experience in the industry first. Clooney began quizzing her about what she wanted to do and offered to come work on one of his upcoming projects that will shoot in Italy.

	Clooney also struck a philosophical note as he remembered, with visible emotion, the death of his sister from cancer last year and being with her in her final moments.

	“She died very quickly, and I was with her when she died. And there was this feeling, being with her, holding her hand when she died, understanding how brief all of this is. It was minutes ago that she and I were little kids together; Minutes ago we were holding hands as little kids,” he said.

	“Time goes fast. All of this. And so we have to find nothing but joy,” he continued.

schema.headline: George Clooney Remembers ‘Mortgaging His House’ for ‘Good Night and Good Luck,’ Praises ‘Badass’ Wife Amal and Offers Aspiring Filmmaker a Job at Venice Masterclass

title: Rosie O’Donnell Meets With Epstein Survivors and Sings ‘I Am Woman’: ‘I’m Sorry That Our Country Is So F—ed Up’
description: Rosie O’Donnell is showing support to survivors of Jeffrey Epstein‘s sexual abuse and sex trafficking. In a new video posted to her Instagram, O’Don
body:
Rosie O’Donnell is showing support to survivors of Jeffrey Epstein‘s sexual abuse and sex trafficking. In a new video posted to her Instagram, O’Donnell met with several survivors and sang a rendition of Helen Reddy’s “I Am Woman” together.

	“I know it’s been very hard for you and with very little support,” O’Donnell tells the survivors. “And I’m sorry that our country is so fucked up that this is what you have to live through, because you are all heroes. And you’re going to change how the world deals with child sex abuse.”
	

	Dressed in all white, the group of women stood side by side, raising their fists while singing the moving lyrics. O’Donnell ended the video with pictures of the survivors when they were younger before showing the words “Support Survivors,” followed by “The Epstein Files.”


	“After the corrupt AG (Trump’s former personal lawyer) stated no men would be charged in the Epstein files — despite mountains of evidence — I called some Epstein survivors [and] asked them to sing with me a powerful Helen Reddy song that taught me at 10 years old to use my voice,” O’Donnell wrote in her caption.

	The former host of “The Rosie O’Donnell Show” and “The View” recently took over as a week-long host of “Jimmy Kimmel Live” in August, where she didn’t hold back on her thoughts about President Trump. 

	“I’ve been living in Ireland for the past two years because of ‘Mango Mussolini,’ she joked during her monologue. “I read that Project 2025 and said, ‘Gotta get myself out of here!’ And I decided to go to Ireland where people are driven to drink regardless of who’s running their country.”
	

	Kimmel was swept up in yet another controversy with the Trump administration earlier this year after the president launched a campaign to get the late-night host fired over jokes about his wife Melania.

	“I support [Kimmel] in what he’s doing with the First Amendment, and our ability as entertainers and citizens to speak out against our government that’s enshrined in the Founding Fathers’ writings about our government, so I think he’s fantastic,” O’Donnell previously told Variety. “And I wish that Stephen Colbert had the same kind of support when it happened to him, because he shouldn’t be gone either.”

schema.headline: Rosie O’Donnell Meets With Epstein Survivors and Sings ‘I Am Woman’: ‘I’m Sorry That Our Country Is So F—ed Up’

title: Hsin Hsuan Yeh Presents ‘The River Within You’ in Venice, an Immersive VR Experience That Navigates Loss, Grief and Letting Go
description: Taiwanese animation director Hsin Hsuan Yeh (“Sense of Nowhere”) is in pre-production on “The River Within You,” an immersive VR experience explorin
body:
Taiwanese animation director Hsin Hsuan Yeh (“Sense of Nowhere”) is in pre-production on “The River Within You,” an immersive VR experience exploring the connection between holding on to the memory of someone lost and finding the strength to let them go. Yeh will present the project at the 13th Venice Production Bridge’s Gap-Financing Market, running Sept. 4-6.

	Told from the perspective of a grandmother who has just died, the story begins as a butterfly guides her soul toward its final resting place: an ocean made of tears. But when her grieving granddaughter’s tear falls onto her body, the grandmother is pulled into a dissolving world of their shared memories, forcing her to journey backwards through their joyful moments before either can move on.
	

	The premise draws on a Taiwanese folk belief that a living person’s tears falling upon the deceased can prevent their soul from finding rest. The tale asks whether, when death frightens us because no new memories can be made, returning to those we already share can become a way of saying goodbye.


	“My grandmother had terminal cancer,” the director tells Variety. “When I came back to Taiwan to see her, she could no longer speak. In my memories, she had always been this happy, optimistic person who was constantly laughing. But after she passed away, somehow I could only remember her as she was during those final days.”

	“The River Within You” grew out of Yeh’s own sense of being stuck – and of the unfairness of grief, which can reduce a lifetime to its final days, allowing hardship to overshadow the person who existed before them. By journeying back to happier moments, she wanted to reclaim that person from a past grief had seemingly erased. “Even though I can’t bring the person back, I can bring back who they were,” she says. “And perhaps remind those still living to cherish both the time they had together and the time they have now.”
	

	For producer Hsia Hsien Chao, the project marks her first time using VR to explore life, death and bereavement. “The story Hsin wants to tell through this immersive experience can resonate anywhere because it comes from something deeply personal,” Chao says. “Even though it draws on a Taiwanese folk belief, the emotions behind it are universal.”

	The 30-minute solo, seated experience places audiences in the grandmother’s perspective as they solve puzzles intended to help her granddaughter work through her grief and ultimately let go. Drawn from Yeh’s own memories with her grandmother, the challenges turn personal recollections into interactive encounters.

	Central to navigating them is hand tracking, transforming touch into both a narrative and emotional device. “What we touch determines what we feel,” the director says. “I wanted to incorporate that into the story because it is deeply connected to how we experience grief – to the way we touch and hold onto the belongings of someone who has died.”

	That sense of human touch extends to the project’s visual language. Photogrammetry-scanned clay models combined with CGI animation preserve tactile textures, bringing handcrafted warmth to the visuals. “VR can feel quite digital and a little isolating, so I want people to feel as though they can almost reach out and touch something,” Yeh says.

schema.headline: Hsin Hsuan Yeh Presents ‘The River Within You’ in Venice, an Immersive VR Experience That Navigates Loss, Grief and Letting Go

title: Alex Witt Has Wisdom: How MS NOW Anchor Lasted Nearly 30 Years in Cable News
description:
The Mayor of Weekends at MS NOW is entering the final days of her term.

	No one elected Alex Witt to public office, but the MS NOW (and MSNBC) vete
body:
The Mayor of Weekends at MS NOW is entering the final days of her term.

	No one elected Alex Witt to public office, but the MS NOW (and MSNBC) veteran has quietly held court on camera on Saturday and Sunday afternoons — in various permutations and formats — for more than two decades. When colleague Alicia Melendez first came to the cable-news outlet, now part of Versant Media, she anchored a weekend slot and turned to Witt  — to whom she gave the ersatz title — for advice, like how to get the makeup she wanted. Witt was able to leverage her Saturday and Sunday experience to help.  “They’re going to hear you now,” Witt says she told her. “Just hang on.”
	

	The Mayor is about to leave.  After joining MSNBC in 1999, she will anchor her last program on September 6 — this Saturday — then fill in on various daytime hours through the rest of the year.


	Ask the average MS NOW viewer which anchors work there, and chances are they’ll talk about Rachel Maddow, Lawrence O’Donnell or Ari Melber. But Alex Witt, by dint of her longevity and her hunker-down-and-do-it style, is right up there, even if weekends aren’t seen as the glitziest time on the schedule. And yet, viewers tend to watch on weekends with fewer distractions and for longer periods of time.  Director Aaron Sorkin would watch Witt regularly and email her for months before asking her to work as a consultant on his HBO series, “The Newsroom.” Actor Rami Malek once ran up to her at a festival to tell her he was an avid viewer.

	“We deliver the same news as everyone else,” says Witt, during a recent visit at MS NOW’s New York headquarters, about working weekends.
	

	Witt was anchoring on a weekend when the U.S. ousted Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro from power earlier this year, and when Saddam Hussein in 2002 submitted an official declaration that Iraq had no weapons of mass destruction. Over the years, says Witt, “there has been a lot on weekends.”

	Her looming departure may be one of the last of its kind. Few people stick with cable news jobs for such a long period of time, and, as the economics of the business change, fewer still may be able to do so. At MS NOW, only correspondent Chris Jansing comes close to matching Witt’s staying power. At Fox News Channel, veteran Neal Cavuto is gone, with Sean Hannity, Brian Kilmeade and Steve Doocy among those who have stayed on the schedule since the network’s early years. Wolf Blitzer, Christiane Amanpour and Anderson Cooper are among the stalwarts at CNN.

	Now there are fewer journalists with such a pedigree, and their number is likely to winnow further. Younger journalists have “all the different, shiny new objects and things” to ply their craft in new venues, says Witt, and the days of working for a single company for an entire career are largely gone. Will others match her durability in years to come? “I think it will be a very rare thing,” she says. “I don’t know that the likes of this comes along again.”

	She attributes her longevity to a focus on delivering the news to the exclusion of many other things. Her Mayor title is purely ceremonial.  “I’ve never played politics and never sought the limelight. I’m the strangest person ever to be on TV. I can’t do my makeup. Trust me, you will not recognize me if you pass me on the street,” she says. “I don’t care about that stuff. I just love the news.” 

	She also has longstanding ties with the people who make her show work behind the scenes. Witt has been paired with the same executive producer, Nick Kovijanic, for years. “He’s my right arm. We finish each other’s sentences,” says Witt, and the two bicker endlessly. “He’ll push the button and he’ll go, ‘Hey, Alex, here’s what we’re gonna do. And I’ll be like, ‘Shut up, get out of my ear. I know what we’re gonna do,” an exchange she equates to “Mom and Dad fighting again.” Kovijanic was supposed to retire in July, but Witt asked him if he would stay on for just a little longer, until her last full show. He agreed. She became a little emotional when speaking about him.
	

	MS NOW may miss her. The network has made all sorts of programming and scheduling changes over the years on weekends, but few if any of them delivered better ratings than the hours Witt anchored, according to two people familiar with operations at predecessor MSNBC. One of these people says Witt has developed a “stickiness” with audiences that will be hard to emulate. Antonia Hylton will take over the weekend-news duties, which Witt sees as a coming-full-circle moment. Before Witt started working weekend hours on MSNBC, they were led by Soledad O’Brien, who is Hylton’s aunt.

	When Witt left college, she never saw herself as someone who would be on camera. She worked as a producer at California stations like KCBS and KNBC, and made her way to a field producer role at NBC’s “Today.” Someone there advised her to look at on-camera jobs and Witt found a spot at KCBA, a northern-California station launched by husband-and-wife journalists.

	When she got married and had a son, Witt decided to focus on motherhood. Her then-husband, also a journalist, got a job at CBS in New York and within a few years, she found herself watching reports about TWA Flight 800, the airplane that exploded after taking off from Kennedy International Airport in New York, and wanting to get back into the business. She landed a freelance job at Fox’s WNYW in New York and then a job anchoring overnights at MSNBC in 1999, thanks to a connection with Eric Sorenson, then the president, whom Witt had known at KCBS. During her time at the network, she has also anchored daytime shows with multiple anchors and even “Way Too Early,” the crack-of-dawn program that precedes “Morning Joe.”

	“Every time I’ve switched positions, I just embrace the hours and go for it,” Witt says. But once she landed on weekends, she never let them go.

	That put-your-head-down attitude has helped her do something she may never have intended. In a sector quickly going through wrenching change, Witt on weekends has dug a groove, becoming a cultural touchstone for her audience — something that can’t be done, at least not yet, with a start-up newsletter or a torrent of social-media likes. “Even in a world where digital is king and social media is the currency, she just did the news. And the audience loved her for it,” says one of the people familiar with MSNBC operations. “That was the key to her longevity.”
	

	Witt likes to ask questions, but rarely puts herself in a position where she must answer a lot of them. She hasn’t done many of the glitzy magazine profiles that are de rigueur for TV-news anchors, and she doesn’t court much attention off camera. When she leaves MS NOW for good, she expects to return to her roots in California, where she might try her hand at writing a book, or teaching, or a bunch of other activities.

	All she wanted to do, she says, is connect with a viewer at home. “I strive to do a really good job. Consistency, I know, helps. And I think I look at the camera lens like I’m talking to you.  It’s one person. I’ve never thought about the numbers. When my parents were alive, it was my parents. I just wanted to talk to them,” says Witt. “And I don’t know, I guess it worked.”

schema.headline: Alex Witt Has Wisdom: How MS NOW Anchor Lasted Nearly 30 Years in Cable News

title: Disney Star Carla Jeffery's Brother Shares the Touching Text He Sent Her
description:
Disney Star Carla Jeffery
                          Brother Reveals Emotional Text
body:
Disney Star Carla Jeffery
                          Brother Reveals Emotional Text
                          Sent Prior to Tragic Death
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 3, 2026
                            10:45 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Carla Jeffery's brother is grieving his sister's tragic death by sharing a touching text he had sent her.
      
    
            Carlon Jeffery took to Instagram to reveal he had texted the Disney alum, asking her to call him back. Carlon wrote ... "I was just calling to see how your day went! I love you to the moon & back sis."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            He went on to give her words of encouragement, writing ... "I just want you to know how proud I am of you. Your resilience, your grace, your infectious smile that lights up a room. You are truly a light that shines bright."
      
    
            Carlon continued by telling Carla to keep her head up when things get tough, saying ... "Don't let anyone.. dim that light.. even yourself. The light you carry is special and must be protected at all times."
      
    
            He concluded ... "You are the best sister a brother could ask for. I pray we continue to grow closer to one another along this journey. I got your back in this life and the next."
      
    
            It's unclear when exactly Carlon sent this message -- the screenshot cut off any sort of date and time stamp -- but it seems to be from before Carla died.
      
    
            As you know, Carla's talent agency announced she died on Tuesday ... but so far, no word on her cause or manner of death. A family spokesperson tells us they're still awaiting autopsy, however they deny all rumors that Carla did drugs.

title: Musician, Pregnant Wife and 3-Year-Old Daughter Shot to Death in Mexico
description:
Mexican Musician
                          Executed With Pregnant Wife And 3-Year-Old Daughter ..
body:
Mexican Musician
                          Executed With Pregnant Wife And 3-Year-Old Daughter ...
                          6-Year-Old Boy Spared
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 3, 2026
                            6:39 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 3, 2026
                                10:58 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A rock musician was shot to death and found Tuesday in Mexico, along with most of his family, including his pregnant wife and 3-year-old daughter, according to CNN.
      
    
            The news outlet reported that Jonathan Meléndez, a 35-year-old keyboardist for indie rock band Camilo Séptimo, was gunned down with his wife, Ana Paula, 35, who was 4 months pregnant, inside their upscale home in Mexico City.
      
    
            Melendez's young daughter was also fatally shot along with her 21-year-old nanny, CNN said, citing the Mexico Attorney General’s Office.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Attorney General said 3 of the victims -- including the daughter -- were shot in the backs of their heads, while a fourth victim was shot in the back.
      
    
            The AG also said 2 victims had their hands tied, and the family dog was found dead with its legs bound. A 6-year-old boy was found unharmed at the scene.
      
    
            Police arrested two men in connection with the murders -- and prosecutors say one suspect used his relationship with one of the victims to enter the home.
